title: Dispatch From Horse Nation
author: Alyse Burnside
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/south-dakota-
final-522-1-680x453.jpeg)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/06/21/dispatch-
from-horse-nation/)

Joelyn and I talked through the bars on the stall windows as we shoveled
manure into large buckets. We had gotten to know each other one Saturday
morning after another, swapping stories while hoisting heavy buckets of horse
shit into a small John Deere tractor at the barn where I worked and he
volunteered each weekend. He’s telling me about a trip he took to Pine Ridge
Reservation, where he went to photograph Indian Relay Races.

“It’s incredible watching the racers," he says, “They run down the track to
their horse bareback, leap onto them from the ground, then take off running.”
He held his phone out to show me a picture of a jockey who wore a purple
folded bandana around his forehead, his hair whipping in the wind. He smiled
through gritted teeth, his eyes were studded with a steely desire. He was mid-
leap, soaring through the air onto his horse. They were already running, all
six legs suspended, a plume of dust behind them. He and a few of the other
jockeys rode for [“The Brew Crew,”](https://www.facebook.com/BrewCrewRelay/)
Pine Ridge’s relay team, owned by a Lakota horseman named Stan Brewer, and
they worked as wranglers at Sage to Saddle in the off-season. Sage to Saddle
is a non-profit started by Stan and Nate Bressler as an effort to teach Lakota
kids on the reservation to ride and to reconnect them to their culture as
horse people.

The image of the jockey on Joelyn’s phone stuck with me, and a few months
later, I was on a plane to South Dakota, looking out my cloudy porthole as we
descended into Rapid City. I had come for the week to meet Joelyn, to watch
Stan’s jockeys work their horses ahead of racing season, and to see the work
Sage to Saddle is doing for the kids in Pine Ridge. Joelyn had invited me
partly because I’m a horse person but also because I’m a writer – he hoped I
might be able to write about the program, bring some attention to it, and
maybe even help them raise a little money.

I drove my rental car two hours south to Pine Ridge, past fields of horses,
casinos, RV parks, roadside restaurants, and towering bluffs. I drove with the
windows down, exhilarated by the open roads. When I got to Pine Ridge, I
turned onto the Oyate Trail, a two-lane highway running along the Nebraska
panhandle through the southern half of the reservation. The hills seemed to go
on forever, with little but land and sky breaking the horizon. Cattle and
horses grazed freely in small herds washed in gold light. I pulled over to
watch a few feral dogs root through a ditch before running off together deep
into the tall prairie grass that ran along the highway.

I turned onto a gravel road as I got closer to the ranch. Outside my window,
FEMA trailers were scattered across the fields in all stages of ruin. It was
hard to tell which ones were inhabited. Car tires sat on most of the roofs,
weighing them down so they didn’t blow away in the bad windstorms, which are
relentless throughout the plains, but wreak particular havoc on the
insubstantial Pine Ridge infrastructure. Some of the trailers I drove past had
their roofs completely torn off, walls stripped of siding, or blown in
entirely. A few miles down the gravel path towards Stan’s ranch, I came upon a
horse in the middle of the road. Jet black with a white snip and two white
socks. He turned to stare for a minute, walked over to my window, then ambled
down into the ditch to graze. Nearby, a patch of barbed wire fence had been
flattened to the ground, and a bay and white Paint stood next to a mule on the
other side, too cautious to cross.

I plugged Stan’s GPS coordinates into my phone, but didn't get cell service.
There aren’t really addresses in this part of the reservation, just markers. I
pulled out the notebook where I’d jotted down instructions from Joelyn. Drive
across four cattle guards and one black gate until I reach a driveway with a
large wooden stump, where I’m to pull off the gravel road and onto a winding
dirt road leading to the ranch. Three small dogs begin to circle the car as I
pull into the driveway – a small fat bulldog named Sally, a beagle with
sagging red eyes named Hazel, and a black and white border collie with one
blue eye named Dandy. I parked behind a large horse trailer and welcomed the
barking dogs into my outstretched arms. Nate stepped out of the camper,
waving. He had a bronzed Florida tan, a compact cowboy body, and a thick
mustache. He wore a tan cowboy hat, round metal frames, and a dark brown
Carhartt jacket. He looked like so many of the cowboys I’ve met in my life,
walking as though he were still in the saddle.

I shook his hand, and then we hugged. Nate opened his arms out toward the
vista in front of him. Stan’s property stretched out for what seemed like
miles, nothing but sky, tall grass, and pines flanking the hills. Joelyn was
haying Nate’s horses across the gravel driveway. We hug, and I grab a large
flake of hay from the jumbo bale and follow him. Nate introduces me to his
horses, a chestnut named JayJay, a chocolate palomino named Chockie, and a
buckskin named ZeZe. For the past eight years, he’s driven them to Pine Ridge
from Florida, where he lives part of the year. It’s a four-day trip, Nate
says, gesturing toward the stock trailer, “but I can make it in three.” Nate
shows me around his airstream, where he lives on Stan’s property. “I tell my
mom she should be proud of me for having my own place,” he laughs, “it’s got
everything: kitchen, bed, pullout couch, and a small dining nook.”

Like me, Nate was raised in the Midwest but eventually found himself in the
city. He was accustomed to ranch life and spent his childhood around horses.
He went to powwows with his aunt and felt a connection to Native culture from
a young age. At 18, he began working with Native kids, while living in
Arizona, and has worked with kids ever since. He spent the first part of his
career as an archaeologist before turning to photography full-time. He’d lived
in New York for a few years, working as a freelance photographer, when he
first came to Pine Ridge on assignment for _Outside Magazine_ in 2016.
_Outside_ was doing a piece on Pine Ridge’s Indian Relay Racing team, and the
death of their jockey Hermis Tall. Tall was one of the most legendary ~~r~~
acers in the history of the sport. Before his death, he’d led the Brew Crew to
the championships three years in a row. Nate followed the Brew Crew for weeks
as they began their first season without Tall.

He got to know Stan and his racers intimately. They stayed up each night
talking, and the longer Nate spent with Stan _,_ the more he knew he wasn’t
going to want to leave. He’d watched how hard the racers trained, how
beautiful their relationships with their horses became, and how difficult life
on the reservation could be. If he were to stay, he wanted to find a way to
give back. He imagined a photography campaign, with images of the racers
wheatpasted around the reservation. Something to inspire a bit of hope and
pride, but it didn’t feel like enough. For one, the weather is too extreme,
anything he posted would be destroyed in no time.

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/south-dakota-
final-357-1-680x472.jpeg)

Photograph by Joelyn Dalit.

He was moved by what he experienced spending time with Stan and his uncle
Shorty Brewer, both of whom had been riding their whole lives. They had
dedicated themselves to reconnecting the next generation of kids to their
cultural roots, to horses and the traditional ceremonies that were stolen from
them during colonization. And like Stan and Shorty and the racers, Nate
understood that horses can be a powerful antidote to sadness. No matter how
dark it gets, a horse always sheds just a little light.

On his last day in town, Nate photographed the Brew Crew’s race at the Oglala
Lakota Nation Fair. He told me that as he was setting up his camp that night,
he had a vision. Together with Stan, they would create a place for Lakota kids
to come ride, to learn from one another, and escape, even if just for a little
bit, whatever difficulties their home lives might present. He wanted the
program to serve as a community of Lakota riders, preparing the next
generation to reclaim the sovereign nation that once belonged to them,
practicing the traditional ceremonies that were once taken from them, and
restoring their cultural legacy as a horse nation.

Stan would need a ranch to keep his 200 head of cattle and his horses, an
indoor arena where kids could escape the cold and ride during the winter
months, and they’d need money to sustain it all. “We put it to the universe,
and the universe answered,” Nate said. Only a few months later, the ranch
across the road from Stan’s went up for sale, along with its acres of pasture,
corrals, and a heated indoor arena. Stan got a loan, and Nate put up some of
the money for him to buy it. Soon after, Nate left his photography career,
bought a camper, and relocated to Stan’s ranch.

While summer months are spent on horseback, the brutal South Dakota winters
drive up Pine Ridge’s already staggering suicide rates, with [teen suicide
rates over 150% higher](https://www.re-member.org/pine-ridge-reservation) than
the national average. Many residents lack [reliable
heat](https://www.onespiritlakota.org/post/fighting-the-deadly-cold-on-pine-
ridge-reservation) during these brutally cold winters, exacerbating all the
other difficulties of life on the reservation. It was crucial to Nate that
kids have a place to be with horses during these long, isolating winters. They
employed the Brew Crew racers as wranglers, in the off-season and began
developing partnerships with local schools so they could ensure kids would
have something to do when they weren’t in class and that they would have
somewhere safe to go, somewhere with electricity and running water, which
homes do not always have on the reservation. Anyone can be part of Sage to
Saddle, but there are conditions they must meet: they must attend school, stay
sober, and stay out of jail.

Pine Ridge is defined to most outsiders by its staggering statistics–as one of
the [poorest places](https://www.census.gov/library/stories/2023/12/poverty-
rates-by-county.html) in America, with the [highest infant mortality
rates](https://bearproject.net/facts-about-pine-ridge/), the [highest
unemployment rates](https://www.cnn.com/2025/11/07/economy/us-pine-ridge-
oglala-sioux-snap-shutdown), and [one of the
lowest](https://southdakotasearchlight.com/2025/02/03/race-and-place-can-
contribute-to-shorter-lives-research-suggests/) life expectancies. Most
Americans will never go to Pine Ridge, or any reservation for that matter, but
when outsiders do, it is often just to document. To film, photograph, record,
or write about the bleakness. To fetishize remarkable resilience, or to yearn
for cultural identity. I, too, had come to document, just as Nate and Joelyn
had. I’d come to write about the vital relationship between horses and people
and to understand the particular and enduring bond between horses and the
Oglala Lakota, set against the history of colonial violence. I had come as a
writer and a horse person, trying to find a way to be useful in a place that
had no particular need for me.

⥈

I’d been on the reservation for maybe an hour before we got in Nate’s truck
and left. There aren’t many restaurants on the reservation, so we drove across
the border into Nebraska for breakfast at a diner called the _Twisted Turtle._
Nate makes a show of telling the server that Joelyn and I are visiting from
New York City. I remind him I was born just one state over. I drink three cups
of black coffee and devour a thick stack of pancakes. Joelyn talks about
watching The Brew Crew race a few summers before, when he’d photographed the
World Championships and met Nate for the first time.

After breakfast, Nate drove us past the Pine Ridge Sanitation Center, which
offers one of the few jobs available on the reservation. With [over
half](https://data.census.gov/profile/Pine_Ridge_Reservation,_SD--
NE?g=2500000US2810#income-and-poverty) of the population living in poverty and
unemployment rates as high as [89%](https://indianyouth.org/combatting-pine-
ridge-reservation-poverty-2023/), jobs like these are highly sought after.
Pine Ridge is [one of the
largest](https://www.oglala.gov/https://www.oglala.gov/) reservations in the
U.S., at 3500 square miles. We spent all day driving the length of its
southern edge, through Porcupine, Manderson, Whiteclay, Wanblee, and finally
north, up to the Badlands. Nate pointed things out while we drove. We passed
the skate park, designed and built by a Lakota skater, with backing from Vans,
the Tony Hawk Foundation, and Pearl Jam bassist, Jeff Ament. A group of young
men filmed as a teen caught the lip of his board onto a metal rail, grinds
down it, then jumps off, his board landing a few feet away in a clatter.

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/south-
dakota-29-04-680x453.jpeg)

Photograph by Joelyn Dalit.

In town, Nate waves to people as we pass, explaining how so-and-so is related
to a Sage kid, or a Brew Crew racer. On the highway, we pass a large modernist
building, all concrete and dark-plated glass, set back off the highway,
surrounded by a parking lot. Now a Lakota cultural center, it was once a
Jesuit boarding school called [Red Cloud Indian
School](https://mahpiyaluta.org/about-us/our-history/), founded in 1888 after
the Massacre at Wounded Knee. Despite being established by the Jesuits at the
request of Chief Red Cloud, in order to teach Lakota children to read and
write, it operated like other Indian boarding schools, with an assimilationist
mission to strip Lakota children of their language and culture, and separate
them from their families. Driving through Pine Ridge, this history looms just
beyond the present like an incessant shadow.

We drove through the southern tip of Badlands National Park. We wound through
towering rock faces, in shades of blush, umber, and bright orange, some
striated with ferrous rings. We pulled over at a lookout spot and walked to
the edge of the cliff, which seemed to drop for miles below. Bighorn sheep
balanced on protruding cliffs, making their way down the cascading rocks that
formed a staircase to the valley of sand sculptures below, where bright orange
hoodoos grow upward toward the sky, amid the vast canyons layered with reds,
pinks, even streaks of blue. I walked through the sandy coves of the cliff
face and ran my hand along mottled walls, reaching inside small crevices to
collect the dust.

Just across the highway, Pronghorn clipped through lush grasses toward the
pine-clad mountains of the Black Hills. The Black Hills, which the Lakota call
_Ȟe Sápa_ are the spiritual center of the universe for the Lakota people. It
was the hills that birthed the Lakota people from the underworld, where they
were guided into the world by the spirits of ancestors and the bison. It is
believed that the hills are mirrors to the heavens, aligning with the cosmos,
creating a multidimensional spiritual grid across the landscape.

It was also where, during the summer of 1874, while traveling with [Custer’s
7th Cavalry](https://www.nps.gov/libi/learn/historyculture/7th-cavalry.htm), a
prospector named Horatio Ross struck gold at French Creek. When reports of his
finding made national headlines, the [Black Hills Gold
Rush](https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/americanexperience/features/custer-timeline/)
began when thousands of prospectors flooded the Lakota’s sovereign land.

We drove a few miles to the Badlands Visitor Center to pee. Dandy and Bud
hopped out of the cab and lifted their legs on a large boulder at the base of
an American flag ripping in the wind. Inside, I browsed souvenirs: a baseball
hat with a black-footed ferret, bison jerky, postcards of spectacular vistas,
bison rattlesnakes, colorful kiddie compasses, a small burlap sack of candied
gold.

Before we head back to Stan’s, we drive to a little town called Interior,
which looks like an old western movie set, with an abandoned theater, two
saloons, and a white clapboard church. We go to a saloon called “The Wagon
Wheel,” with hitching posts outside. Inside, the bar is dimly lit, a man sits
alone in a booth watching grainy football replays from the TV hung in the
corner, two cowboys shoot pool in the middle of the room. We grab stools
around the bar, which has a long mirrored wall, and Christmas lights strung
from its old, wooden eaves. We ordered a round of red beers—tomato juice and
watery beers, and bags of corn chips.

⥈

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/word-
image-415946-1.jpeg)

Arianna and horse, photograph by Alyse Burnside.

The next day, I arrived at the barn around two to help get the horses ready
for the first day of the Sage to Saddle afterschool program.

I wander into the arena to see the Brew Crew racehorses in their holding
stalls. A tall, lean chestnut hangs his head over his stall door, puts his
face close to mine, and blows hot air onto my back. Nate introduces me to Stan
and to Sage’s wranglers: Kalijah, Davis, Joe, and Maria. Kalijah and Davis hop
on a four-wheeler and ride up the hill to grab a few horses from the far
paddocks. “Joelyn, get your camera out so you can photograph them riding in
with the horses,” Nate says, “It’s a sight to watch them all ride down
together.” I take my cell phone out and record as Davis rides Nate’s chocolate
Palomino, Chalkie, down the hill, ponying three horses behind him.

Soon after, the low growl of the four-wheeler grows louder, and Kalijah turns
down the hill holding two leadropes, one horse at each side of his quad. Joe
and his girlfriend Maria hop onto their horses in a nearby pasture, jumping
from the ground, wrapping their arms around their horses’ necks as they move
off. Maria rides up next to a stocky bay horse, swings a rope around his neck,
and halters him. They ride down the hill, horses in hand like a gallant
procession. Joelyn’s shutter clicks in double-time with the sound of hooves on
the gravel.

The wranglers tie the horses to posts in the arena. Nate hops in a Sprinter
van and head to pick up the Sage kids from school on the other side of the
reservation, nearly an hour away. Joelyn, Stan, and I help the wranglers get
the horses ready. Stan is friendly, with a youthful warm smile. He is the kind
of guy you can tell has a good sense of humor even if you never hear him crack
a joke. We make a little small talk, but he is focused on the horses and the
kids. He keeps moving, busying himself trimming one of the pony’s hooves,
haying the Thoroughbreds, and setting up the arena for the day’s lesson. When
the horses are tacked, we polish our cowboy boots and wait for the kids to
arrive.

Davis sets up a plastic steer and practices roping. He flicks his lasso over
his head, turning it back on itself before casting it out in front of him. The
waxy rope makes a _swish_ as it falls over the steer’s head, then a _ziiippp_
when he pulls it back, taut around the steer’s horns. When he misses, the rope
makes a hard _thwack_ against the plastic, and Davis sucks air through his
teeth. I sit on a bench next to two barn kittens huddled together on a dusty
office chair. Joe begins to tell stories. He’s the performer of the group. His
personality is made even bigger in comparison to the other wranglers, whose
quiet temperaments leave room for him to take the stage. His girlfriend Maria,
sits next to him, smirking, holding the beagle on her lap, interjecting at
times to tease him gently or add her own details. Kalijah cracks sunflower
seeds in his lap, shimmying loose shells onto the ground.

I recognized Joe immediately from Joelyn’s photos. I began asking him about
racing, how long he’d been with the Brewer team, if he had a favorite horse,
and if he ever felt afraid hopping wildly from horse to horse. “I think she
might be my favorite,” he said, pointing at a sinewy chestnut with his head
hanging out his stall window, “Fast as fuck!”

Unlike in typical racing where a jockey races one horse for the length of a
race, in a relay, a jockey rides three horses, each for a single lap, jumping
off one and immediately onto the next. The loud crack of a gun sounds, and the
racers run to their horse’s side, place their hands on their horse’s withers
as they leap into the air and hurdle onto them, as though they were throwing
themselves over a fence. Sometimes they’d mount by “ass-hopping,” running up
behind the horse, placing their hands on either side of their hind, and
leapfrogging onto their horse’s back. As they mount, the handlers struggle to
hold the horses back, their whole bodies pulsing with energy. They pull
against the metal bit in their mouth, swing their hind ends into one another
as though to kick, and some begin to rear, lifting their front ends into the
air. It is a spectacle to see bodies colliding, energy coming together, and
taking off.

The jockeys ride bareback, sometimes at over 35 miles an hour. They often
dress in traditional regalia,–breechcloth, beaded moccasins, and warbonnets.
They wear team jerseys or ride bare-chested. They mark their horses with
symbols painted in colored chalk. A circle painted around their horse’s eye
heightens their instincts, stripes grant them speed, a handprint grants them
protection and safe return from battle.

Occasionally, the racers overshoot their mounts and hurdle right over their
horse’s back, tumbling to the ground. Sometimes the muggers fail to catch an
incoming horse, causing a pile-up, sometimes jockeys get trampled. Even
winning could be dangerous.

I’d seen videos of Joe racing before I came. I’d seen him leaping wildly onto
and off his horses, sometimes ass-hopping. I’d watched with great anxiety as
he barreled down the track, thrusting his hands forward with each stride, his
legs wrapped around his horse’s barrel. I asked him if he’d ever been injured
in a race, and he lit up excitedly, leaned forward in his chair, and began to
tell a story.

Once, while making his way to the winner’s circle, Joe began to do a
celebratory dance, scaring a young Thoroughbred. The horse spun around and
double-barreled him, kicking him in the stomach until he doubled over. He
picked himself off the ground and posed for his victory photos. At his team’s
urging, he visited the medic tent, where he was brushed off and told to take
some Aspirin for his pain. It was a Lakota nurse who had seen the accident,
who insisted he go to the hospital to be checked for internal bleeding. A
decision that ultimately saved his life. He laughs now as he tells the
story—in that same effervescent, almost maniacal way he’s told all the stories
I’ve heard since I arrived—the sad, hysterical, and absolutely terrifying.

He was taken to a nearby hospital, then life-flighted to Rapid City for
emergency surgery to stop his internal bleeding. By this point, Joe is so
excited his smile takes up almost his whole face. He pulls his t-shirt up to
reveal a scar running from his left hipbone to his right ribcage. “Check this
shit out,” he says. Maria rolls her eyes and laughs along with us, even though
I’m sure she’s heard this story a million times by now. She laughs, as we do,
even though the story sounds terrifying to me.

“Were you afraid to race after that?” I ask stupidly. “Hell nah! I’m a goddamn
maniac,” he yells, and we roar. “For real, though, life is short for Indian
men, so I figure why the hell not race? Why not die doing this?” His eyes
harden a bit, “I hit middle age at 18. I’m a geezer already!” He hunches
forward a bit, as though pushing his invisible walker, making his voice
pinched like an old man. I have laughed all the air out of my lungs. We are
still laughing, the muscles in my face begin to cramp. Joe laughs the most and
the loudest. He wraps his arm around his stomach and doubles over. His
laughter becomes squeaky, like a deflating balloon, then devolves into gasps
for air. “I’m not even kidding,” he says one last time, and we laugh all over
again.

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/south-dakota-
final-375-1-680x506.jpeg)

Photograph by Joelyn Dalit.

When the kids arrive, they set their backpacks down on a bench lining the
arena wall. Nate tells them there are visitors from New York City who have
come all the way to see them ride. I tell them that it is illegal to gallop a
horse in the city, one of the few horse facts I can bring that might surprise
them. The kids are shocked, but Stan and the wranglers find this particularly
outrageous. “I’d be getting pulled over all the time,” Kalijah says, “Yeah, I
can’t go there,” Davis agrees. The kids begin to joke, “please officer, I
didn’t know how fast I was riding,” one girl begs. A few of the kids seem
intrigued by the idea of the city, but most of them don’t. We all stand and
form a circle in front of the horses. Each ride begins with a ceremonial
saging. Nate lights a small bundle of sage in an Abalone shell. He gathers the
curling smoke with a cupped hand, and raises it up over his head. We pass it
around the circle, each of us dropping it over ourselves like a veil of
protection. Once the circle is completed, the kids put on their riding helmets
and find their horse.

Stan tells me I can ride one of the ponies called Peggy. A gelding with a
long, crimped mane and light bay coat. “He’s a gelding named Peggy, kind of
like ‘A Boy Named Sue,’” Stan laughs. Peggy pushes his nose into my pockets
looking for treats. I scratch his shoulder, and he extends his neck and his
top lip twitches, grooming the air.

The wranglers help the kids mount their horses. Everyone else is riding full-
sized horses, and I only come up to their knees on Peggy. While he might be
child-sized, he isn’t as trustworthy as he’d need to be for kid riders. I take
him around the ring with the others. We trot a few laps in each direction,
then I lope him around a bit, and he throws his head down, arching his back to
throw a few crowhops, lifting his hind end only slightly off the ground. At
his size, the hops don’t unseat me, but feel as though I’m bouncing on a pogo
stick. One of the girls laughs a little when she sees us hopping together.

We lined our horses up along the arena wall, taking turns riding them through
a chute and over a ground pole raised a foot or so on one side, wedged between
two slats of a metal fence panel. We learned to use our weight in the saddle
to help our horses move over objects on the ground, creating a sense of safety
so that we could clear these obstacles together. The first rider manages
seamlessly, her horse hopping effortlessly over the pole. The second horse
refuses at first, and after a little coaxing, walks over.

Soon it is my turn. Peggy was a roping pony, used to speed and quick turns. He
had a fearless but flighty energy that reminded me of my old horse, Shirley,
whose strong will broke several of my bones, but who was my refuge during the
most difficult moments of my childhood. We make our turn into the chute, and
Peggy starts dancing. I bring my weight out of the saddle and off his back. He
pushes his nose out and lowers his head. Ego takes over a bit, and I think of
how mortifying it would be to be the New Yorker who fell off Peggy the pony.
Peggy surely senses my ego and wants nothing more than to obliterate it. He
would love to be the pony to throw a New Yorker to the ground.

The kids were shy, as preteens tend to be. I was shy too, a bit worried my
presence is an intrusion on their time together. I asked one of the girls
whether she likes riding, and she nodded, a bit bashfully. One thing horses
can teach us is how to communicate beyond words, and watching the kids ride
together, they seemed at home on their horses, and at home together in this
arena.

Nate calls them “Bucky.” “It’s hard to get a lot out of them,” he explains,
“But they like to spend time with their friends, and they like to spend time
with horses, and that’s all I really need to hear.” Some of the kids have
difficult home lives. Many have had loved ones die, and most have seen people
close to them struggle. Time spent riding can be a small reprieve from these
heavy realities, and time spent riding together can make life less isolating.

⥈

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/south-dakota-
final-482-680x453.jpeg)

Photograph by Joelyn Dalit.

Nearly every night, I make the drive from the ranch back to my motel in Hot
Springs in the pitch dark. I look up the Pine Ridge Reddit, which warns me not
to linger after dark because of the high crime rates, but most nights I don’t
pass a single soul. I’m more worried about hitting feral dogs, cattle, or
horses that might wander onto the road.

Instead, it’s my drive into Hot Springs that unsettles me. I’m pulled over
almost immediately, a cop with an unmarked car squeals its sirens, unveiling a
panel of lights at the top of his windshield. The officer walks slowly toward
me, his flashlight beaming through my rearview window. His hulking trunk is
all I see out my driver’s side window. He’s wearing a tight black t-shirt, a
bulletproof vest, a gator pushed down over his neck, his badge, and a blue
brass pin. He looks like he’s on his way to a militia meeting rather than
nightly small-town rounds. He asks me where I’m from and what I’m doing here.
He’s pulled me over because I’m driving a little slowly, seeming a little
lost. I know not to mention the reservation. Instead, I spin a strange story
about visiting my husband’s grandmother in Rapid City, of being awed by my
surroundings and wanting to take them in slowly. I laugh a little, knowing
that despite my anxiety, I will drive away soon with just a warning.

The lodge is motel-style, with doors facing the driveway across from a strip
mall. A large Chevy truck sat in front of my room most nights with a bumper
sticker that read L.G.B.T., which I’d quickly noticed on my first night here.
When I walked closer, I saw that LGBT stood for Liberty. Guns. Beer. Trump.

Each night, I’d park my rental car, take out my dull pocket knife, and dart
across the parking lot to my door, nearly tripping every time on the uneven
concrete. Once inside, I’d push the couch in front of the door and close the
blinds. The room itself was to be expected. A bible on the nightstand, a
painting of cowboys riding over a rocky cliff, and a small mini fridge. The
walls were thin, and the room smelled strongly of sickly sweet Febreze, spring
glade, or lilac sunrise, or some other powdery annihilation.

I called my girlfriend. At some point, I started calling Pine Ridge “The Rez.”
It came out of my mouth easily, but didn’t feel like it belonged to me._“The
Rez,”_ she says, teasing, she’d heard it too.

In the morning, I wake up early and drive through the Black Hills, to Custer,
where the Gold Rush began. As I drive, the terrain turns from lush green hills
to craggy mountains mottled with tall naked pines, charred from wildfire. As I
climbed up the hills, the road began to narrow, and granite rock pillars on
either side of the road closed in around me, massive eroded granite spires
jutting out of the ground like pointed blades. Billboards line the highway
outside of Custer: Mt. Rushmore tours, Wall Drug, “Shoot a Machine Gun Today,”
and Big Thunder Gold Mine.

Now overrun with tourist shops and sham gold panning excursions, this was once
Lakota sovereign land. After the discovery of gold in 1874, white prospectors
pillaged the hills in hopes of striking gold. When Lakota tribal leaders
Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse refused to sell the land that was so sacred to
them, the army set out on a crusade to force them into reservations. In 1876,
in what is now known as the Battle of the Little Bighorn, the Lakota
surrounded the Cavalry and [killed all
210](https://www.history.com/articles/little-bighorn-battle-facts-causes) of
them, including Custer. The battle marked a decisive victory for the Lakota,
but resulted in intensified efforts to separate the Lakota people and confine
them to reservations.

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/south-dakota-
final-475-680x1020.jpeg)

Photograph by Joelyn Dalit.

After the victory at the Battle of the Little Bighorn, the Cavalry also set
out to separate the Lakota from their horses. The Lakota were referred to by
other tribes as “Horse Nation” because horses were the backbone of their
culture, and their innate connection to horses is central to their way of
life. The U.S. Army recognized this power and sought to destroy it. 1876 is
commonly known to Lakota people as “The Year We Lost Our Horses.”
Simultaneously, they launched a crusade to systematically eliminate the
buffalo, the Lakota’s primary food source.

Bereft of their horses, the Lakota were immobilized, and the following year,
Crazy Horse was marched to Fort Robinson, Nebraska, and killed after resisting
orders to surrender his (now starving) tribe to reservation encampments. By
1877, the government had carved the sovereign land into the reservations,
which would become Pine Ridge, Standing Rock, Rosebud, and Cheyenne River. The
Lakota people were separated, confined, and tightly controlled by the US
government.

Back at the ranch, Joelyn watches as Joe works a colt in the round pen. A
beautiful red roan with a rabicano tail, just three and not yet greenbroke.
He’s had a few rides, Joe says, he’s doing alright. The colt lopes around Joe
in circles, his head hanging low to the ground in a sign of cooperation. Joe
stops, and he turns in towards him, walks tentatively to the center of the
ring, and follows Joe as he walks to get a bridle hanging from the gate. Joe
swings his split reins over his saddle horn and puts his foot tentatively in
the stirrup. The colt shuffles a little, then stands still. Joe swings his leg
over the saddle and moves his horse off around the pen without resistance. He
rides with a serious concentration; he sits back in the saddle, his long legs
reaching out a bit in front of him like a cowboy. He’s wearing a red flannel
shirt and dark blue Wranglers. A pair of Oakleys sits on the brim of his hat.
“Hey man, could you take some pictures?” Joe asks Joelyn. All the wranglers
want Joelyn to take professional pictures of them so they can post them to
their Instagrams.

The week moved quickly, and before I knew it, this was my last night. Nate and
Stan had organized a trail ride with some of the Sage to Saddle kids for the
following day. The weather was nice, the sky streaked with purple as the sun
began to set, so I drove the long way back to the motel, along the Black Hills
Scenic Highway to the Buffalo Gap Grassland, listening to KILI, the
reservation’s radio station. A solitary buffalo stood at the side of the road,
the first one I’d ever seen. I pull over a few hundred yards away from him and
open my door.

I kept my distance, but it was difficult to imagine this animal could even
really harm me. Its size was the only thing that felt remotely menacing. It
was much larger than a cow, with humped shoulders and a bushy mane that made
him look like he was wearing a shrug around his neck. By contrast, he had a
slender, virtually hairless backside, which made him seem almost mythic, like
the human bottom of a satyr or centaur. It, he?, stood completely still,
gazing across the highway, over the shrubland that stretched across the
horizon to the base of the black hills. Just when I began to think he wasn’t
real, that maybe he was a stuffed bison placed near the park’s entrance, he
lowered his massive head to the ground and blew air through his leathery
nostrils, picking up a small plume of dust.

I ripped open the plastic wrapping of my vegan jerky, and he turned his glassy
eye on me. He moved like an animatronic dinosaur. Now that I knew he was
alive, I felt the impulse to photograph him, lifted my phone, and took a few
grainy shots. After a few minutes, another car pulled over on the other side
of the highway to take pictures, so I closed my door and drove on.

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/word-
image-415946-2.jpeg)

Lone bison, photograph by Alyse Burnside.

On my last day, I made my final drive from Hot Springs, Marty Robbins crooning
through my speakers, _I’m as free as the breeze, and I ride where I please._
It was early and it would be a full day, but there was so much I would not
see. I felt sad that my trip was ending, and a little conflicted about having
enjoyed myself so much, worried that I was taking something away from my time
and not giving much back in return.

Before heading to the ranch, I stopped at the Wounded Knee Memorial. I drove
to the top of the hill and parked in a small parking lot facing the entrance
to the cemetery, marked by two white-brick pillars connected by a metal arch
with a small, plain crucifix on top.

In 1890, [nearly ¼](https://history.nebraska.gov/the-military-buildup-to-
wounded-knee/) of the U.S. Army was sent to Pine Ridge and Rosebud
reservations to “subdue” what they claimed to fear would become a military
uprising. On December 29th, amid a treacherous blizzard, the U.S. 7th Cavalry,
the same regiment that had been defeated at the Battle of the Little Bighorn,
surrounded Chief Bigfoot and his band of Lakota people at Wounded Knee Creek.
The army ordered the Lakota to surrender their weapons, and a struggle broke
out when one man refused. In the struggle, a shot was fired, and the cavalry
soldiers opened fire on the Lakota, shooting their rifles into the crowd, now
defenseless without their weapons or their horses. They shot cannons from a
nearby hill, slaughtering women and children. The massacre marked the end of
the Indian Wars on the Great Plains. In all, [300
Lakota](https://www.history.com/articles/wounded-knee-massacre-facts) were
killed, their bodies left to freeze in the blizzard, and were buried in a mass
grave.

The ground around the cemetery is arid, and grass struggles to grow in small
patches. Just before the cemetery, a metal plaque painted red with white trim
tells a brief and skewed history of one of the most brutal events in Lakota
history. Like most historical markers, this is a history written from the
victor’s point of view, softening the brutality to a tragic misunderstanding
rather than a genocidal slaughter. The plaque ends with the line, “The wounded
knee battlefield is the site of the ~~last~~ armed conflict between the Sioux
Indians and the United States Army. The word “last” blacked out with spray
paint.

Each December, the Brewer family organizes the Chief Bigfoot Memorial ride, an
arduous 300-mile ride, trial that connects young people to their ancestors,
and an experience that forges a deep bond between riders and their horses. It
begins in Standing Rock, where Chief Sitting Bull was killed on December 15th,
1980, and travels the path his followers fled, toward Wounded Knee, and ends
at the site of the massacre.

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/word-
image-415946-3.jpeg)

Calvin and Sparky, photograph by Alyse Burnside.

When I arrived at the ranch, the wranglers were working with their horses,
practicing moving invisible herds of cows, pivoting, and stopping quickly. In
a few weeks, they’d set out to brand this season’s herd. For now, the babies
lay in piles around the cow pasture, and their mothers grazed a little ways
away.

Joe, Maria, Kalijah, Davis, and another racer named Arianna went to catch
horses. Arianna’s horse was difficult and moved quickly from one pile of hay
in the paddock corner to the next, just before she could grab him. When she
finally did, he began to trot off as she mounted. Joe and Maria laughed as she
pulled herself onto her horse’s back, grabbing a handful of his mane.

Stan’s nephew Calvin and a few Sage kids arrive to ride. We stood in a large
circle and saged ourselves, then rode out of the barn in a long procession.
Calvin was 11, and rode his small black and white Paint pony Sparky bareback,
in his racing bridle. He hopped onto the pony just like the wranglers do, and
rode with the same cowboy posture, his legs long and straight, feet just
slightly in front of him as though coming in for a sliding stop. He told me
he’d been riding as long as he could remember, and had begun racing in the
Junior Relays a few summers ago.

It was only March, but it felt like summer. My face was an angry red and slick
with sweat. Gnats buzzed around Peggy’s face, and he shook his head to throw
them off. The wranglers rode ahead, taking a detour so they could run across
the open field. Their horses pranced and pushed against their bits, but they
held them back until we rounded a bend of trees down a lowland path toward a
creek. Then they cut off to run across the open field. The rest of us rode
together with the dogs running alongside us, the sound of the wranglers ahead,
tearing through the trees, our horses snorting in anticipation, or to force
the bugs from their noses.

A light breeze blew through the creek. Peggy pawed at the water vigorously,
water splashing all around us, soaking my pant legs and the ends of my braids.
He stuck his muzzle into the water to drink, then slapped the water’s surface
with his mouth, blowing bubbles, then pawing again with his other leg. This
was mutual joy, the temporary suspension of vigilance. Each splash of the
water’s surface pulled out any anxiety I might have had, obliterated, even if
momentarily, any mask I might have been wearing. Together in the creek, we
played.

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/word-
image-415946-4-680x907.jpeg)

Kalijah and Pepper, photograph by Alyse Burnside.

The other horses began to paw too, the sound of crashing hooves almost
eclipsing our laughter. Overcome with such genuine pleasure, my eyes begin to
water. Arianna lay back on her horse, hands laced on her stomach, looking up
at the sky as her horse waded slowly into the water. Aubree, one of the Sage
riders, was riding Chockie when he buckled at the knees. He hovered for a
moment before lowering his body into the water, overcome by the irresistible
desire to roll, to feel the water over his shoulders and back. Aubree stepped
off into the waist-deep creek. Nate took hold of her reins and pulled him up
mid-roll as she climbed out of the water, wrung the water from her t-shirt,
and got back on.

As we rode back towards the barn, the horses began to speed up, eager for the
familiarity of home. I felt Peggy’s breath quicken, his body becoming tense
underneath me. Up ahead, the wranglers let their horses run home. The sound of
their horses’ hooves against the tall grass made a deep whirring, like a blade
beating at stalks. Echoes of ecstatic laughter reverberated across the open
field.
